extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of poetics (writers and critics of epic and tragic verse)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and evaluative principles for composing and judging classical tragedy and epic poetry: diction, metre, structure (beginning–middle–end), use of the marvellous, metaphor, and poetic licences. Emphasis on suitability of devices to metre and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode_of_statement/versification_effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode of stating (e.g., versification) matters because it can render things tolerable in verse which would be intolerable in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the same matter stated one way is unattractive but another mode renders it attractive, that mode requires study; versification can alter acceptability and audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosody_and_phonetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Study of the basic sound-units (letters, vowels, semi-vowels, mutes), combinations, and prosodic differences (place of articulation, breathing, length, intonation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences of sound-shape, breathing (hard/soft), length (long/short), and intonation (acute/grave/intermediate) should be studied in Prosody because they affect versification and diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction_should_be_clear_and_not_common
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence of diction is to be clear and not common: clearness (ordinary appellations) vs. choiceness (extraordinary appellations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance ordinary appellations (produce clearness) with extraordinary ones (dialectic names, metaphors, protractions) for stateliness. Avoid making all phrases extraordinary (becomes a riddle) or all dialectic (becomes gibberish). Use licences in moderation; substitution of a single dialectic word can change a line from commonplace to fine (example: Aeschylus vs. Euripides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original_metaphor_as_sign_of_talent
rubrics_metrics.description: The gift of original metaphor is essential and cannot be borrowed; coining metaphors with skill shows ability to see likenesses in things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphors produce pleasure by identifying likeness while allowing difference; images suggesting motion are more effective. Cultivate original metaphors rather than relying solely on borrowed ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types_of_metaphor_and_analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor may transfer names genus→species, species→genus, species→species, or by analogy (B is to A as D to C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calling a cup ‘Dionysus’s Shield’ (cup:shield analogy); using Evening as 'Life's eventide'. Can substitute improper appellation with a negation of a property (e.g., 'Wineless' instead of 'Ares's Cup'). Choose type to suit effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_coined_lengthened_contracted_protracted_words
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetical licences include coined words (invented), lengthened words (long vowel or inserted syllable), contracted words (suppressed part), and protracted/remodelled words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such licences, by differing from the normal, give choiceness while retaining some clearness if related to ordinary appellations. Critics who ridicule these licences may miss their poetic function. Employ with moderation; overuse is ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_overuse_of_licences (riddle_vs_gibberish)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all phrases are metaphors the result is a riddle; if all are dialectic names the result is gibberish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix ordinary and extraordinary forms. Excessive use of licences produces unintelligibility or ludicrous effect; moderation is necessary in all varieties (metaphor, dialectic names, protractions, compounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical_selection_by_metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain lexical ornaments suit particular metres: compounds are most suitable for dithyrambs; dialectic words for hexameters; metaphors for iambics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hexameters admit all varieties and a special vocabulary; iambics, due to imitation of ordinary conversation, suit ordinary appellations, metaphor and euphemism. Put nouns into the centre in hexameters (fix nouns and accommodate metre to them) to study suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement_of_nouns_in_hexameter
rubrics_metrics.description: In hexameters the nouns should often be placed in the centre (make them the fixed element) rather than adjusting them wholly to the metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing by putting nouns in the centre shows the intrinsic beauty of altered forms independent of metrically-required alterations. This helps evaluate whether lexical licences are suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic_structure_whole_chapter_unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic (narrative in hexameters) should be constructed to embrace one whole and complete chapter of life, with beginning, middle, and end — dramatic unity rather than a monotonous chronicle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid monotonous chronicles that merely record many events in a period without directing them toward a single end. Select a chapter and, where useful, use other chapters as episodes (Homer's use of episodes). Limit length so that beginning and end can be grasped in one view; epic may be longer than tragedy but still should present unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic_requires_tragic_varieties_and_factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic should have the same varieties as Tragedy (simple or complex, psychological or emotional) and should include Irony of Fate, Recognition (Disclosure of Mistaken Identity), and Catastrophe; Intelligence and Diction should be of good quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except for Music and Presentation, factors of tragedy apply to epic. Choose construction (e.g., Iliad simple and emotional; Odyssey complex and psychological) to embody these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter_suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a metre appropriate to the work: heroic metre (hexameter) is most sedate and ambitious and therefore suits epic; iambics and trochaics suit motion and dance respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience has shown heroic metre best for long narrative. Attempting a lengthy narrative in other metres has historically failed. Instinct guides metre selection; mixing metres (absurd) should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial_persona_and_narrator_intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; after a brief introduction he should bring characters on who each have distinct personalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize direct authorial declamation; impersonation (speaking through characters) is preferable. This aids dramatic illusion and avoids breaking the fiction's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_marvellous_and_poetic_justice (backgrounded)
rubrics_metrics.description: The marvellous (and poetic justice) may be introduced but should be kept in the background; a plausible impossibility is preferable to an unconvincing possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making unnatural events integral to the plot; if introduced, conceal them by preparation and other fascinations. Poetic justice increases marvel but is difficult on stage; in narrative it is easier to accept. If unnatural elements are used, either thoroughly prepare and emphasize them or keep them in the background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_unaccountable_elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The account should not be made up of unaccountable elements; if any must exist they should be backgrounded and not necessary to the story's intelligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely upon absurd features that the plot would otherwise require; if a feature is introduced and a more intelligible procedure is obviously possible, that is preposterous and undermines the plot's credibility (examples: some episodes in the Odyssey or the Electra's anachronism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_picturesque_detail_for_plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Append details that naturally accompany a fictional element to create illusion: if A entails B in nature, include B so the audience infers A (the fallacy of inferring causation from consistency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention to picturesque details (e.g., Bath-scene) makes a fiction plausible; these details exploit the audience's knowledge of regular accompaniment to infer the main (possibly fictional) event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care_with_diction_in_flat_passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Special care should be taken with diction in 'flat' passages (where there is neither psychology nor reasoning); conversely, over-brilliant diction obscures both psychology and reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve striking diction for passages where it enhances effect; in flat or expositional sections, prefer clarity and restraint to avoid obscuring the intellectual or emotional content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer_plausible_impossibility_over_unconvincing_possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When forced to choose, prefer a plausible impossibility (an impossibility plausibly prepared) to an unconvincing possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience acceptance depends on plausibility; prepare for and justify any violation of ordinary causation rather than presenting weakly-motivated 'possible' events that do not convince.
